question: What is the primary difference between vaccine efficacy and vaccine effectiveness?

options.A: Efficacy is tested on children whereas effectiveness is tested on adults
options.B: Effectiveness looks at cost while efficacy looks at side effects
options.C: Efficacy applies only to viral vaccines while effectiveness applies to bacterial vaccines
options.D: Effectiveness measures real-world protection while efficacy measures controlled trial results

explanation: Controlled clinical trials determine efficacy under ideal circumstances, whereas effectiveness evaluates how well the vaccine works among diverse populations in routine clinical settings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h1)

question: Why is community immunity important in a local healthcare setting?

options.A: It protects vulnerable people who cannot safely receive vaccines
options.B: It guarantees that diseases will never mutate into new strains
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future vaccine booster doses
options.D: It reduces the cost of purchasing cold chain equipment

explanation: High vaccination coverage creates a protective barrier around infants, pregnant women, and sick patients who lack functional immune systems to take vaccines themselves. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h1)

question: How does severe malnutrition affect a child's response to routine immunizations?

options.A: It permanently destroys the injection site tissue
options.B: It speeds up the rate at which vaccines are metabolized
options.C: It impairs antibody production and overall immune response
options.D: It eliminates the need for administering booster shots

explanation: Adequate nutrition supplies the vital components needed for lymphocytes and antibodies to form properly after antigen exposure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h2)

question: A patient with active immunosuppression is most likely to experience what outcome from a live attenuated vaccine?

options.A: Total immunity within twenty four hours of injection
options.B: An unusually high and rapid surge in protective antibodies
options.C: Severe disease manifestations from the vaccine strain itself
options.D: Immediate elimination of the vaccine without any immune memory

explanation: Immunocompromised hosts cannot control weakened live organisms, turning a standard preventive vaccine into a dangerous active infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h2)

question: What happens to liquid vaccines like tetanus toxoid when exposed to freezing temperatures?

options.A: Their expiration date extends by an extra six months
options.B: They transform into live attenuated viral agents
options.C: They become completely inert until heated in a microwave
options.D: They lose potency permanently and cannot be used

explanation: Freezing damages the aluminum adjuvant in toxoid vaccines, causing structural changes that destroy their ability to stimulate protection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h3)

question: What should a nurse do when checking a Vaccine Vial Monitor and finding the inner square is darker than the outer circle?

options.A: Use the vaccine immediately before the color fades further
options.B: Shake the vial vigorously to mix the active ingredients back
options.C: Discard the vial because heat exposure has damaged the vaccine
options.D: Place the vial in a vaccine refrigerator overnight to reset it

explanation: A dark inner square indicates the vaccine has been exposed to excessive heat over time, rendering it unsafe and ineffective for administration. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h3)

question: The primary consequence of administering an intramuscular vaccine into the subcutaneous layer is:

options.A: Complete destruction of the vaccine vial inside the syringe
options.B: Permanent paralysis of the nearest major nerve trunk
options.C: Immediate systemic toxicity from rapid drug absorption
options.D: Reduced immune response and increased local adverse reactions

explanation: Subcutaneous tissue has poorer blood supply than muscle, leading to altered antigen processing and higher rates of local irritation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h4)

question: Why must nurses strictly follow the recommended time intervals between successive vaccine doses?

options.A: To ensure the patient experiences mild fever as proof of efficacy
options.B: To match the reporting requirements of local government authorities
options.C: To prevent the expiration of stock in the clinic pharmacy
options.D: To allow proper maturation of immunological memory cells

explanation: Giving booster doses too early can lead to neutralization of the vaccine antigen by existing circulating antibodies instead of stimulating a strong secondary response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h4)

question: What term describes the delay or refusal of vaccination despite the availability of services?
explanation: Vaccine hesitancy refers to the reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite the availability of vaccination services, driven by complacency, convenience, and confidence issues. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h5)

question: How can community health nurses best address local myths regarding routine childhood immunizations?

options.A: Collaborating with trusted local and religious leaders for education
options.B: Ignoring community concerns and focusing only on administrative records
options.C: Threatening parents with legal action if they miss clinic dates
options.D: Distributing vaccines door-to-door without explaining their purpose

explanation: Involving respected community figures helps dispel rumors and builds authentic trust, which improves acceptance and vaccine uptake. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common logistical barrier to immunization in rural health centers?

options.C: Abundant availability of solar-powered cold rooms

explanation: Most rural primary healthcare facilities face severe shortages of reliable cold storage technology rather than having an abundance of them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h6)

question: What is a missed opportunity for vaccination in a clinical setting?

options.A: A vaccine vial breaking on the floor during preparation for injection
options.B: A parent arriving at the clinic after working hours when doors are locked
options.C: An eligible child visiting a health facility for any reason leaves without receiving needed vaccines
options.D: A nurse forgetting to order new vaccine stock before the expiration date

explanation: Every clinical encounter with a child is an opportunity to check vaccination status and administer any missing doses, preventing gaps in immunity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T70#GNS214_U1_T70_h6)
